title: Afterthoughts and Aftertastes: Dynamics of Psychological Incubation
content: Emotional, motivational, and attentional responses sometimes intensify long after an initial event has ended, despite the absence of further external reinforcement. Such phenomena have been observed across largely separate psychological literatures — from anxiety and craving to romantic infatuation and delusion — often treated as distinct because of their differing content. This paper presents a unified framework by formalising Eysenck’s concept of “incubation” through a minimal modification of the Rescorla–Wagner model of Pavlovian conditioning. By allowing reactivation of internal representations to contribute to subsequent strengthening or weakening, we show that response growth, maintenance, and decay can emerge from a single dynamical system. A representation’s long-term trajectory depends less on the severity of the initial learning episode than on the ongoing competition between internal rehearsal and extinction. We apply this shared computational architecture to post-event processing in social anxiety, anger rumination, incentive sensitization, and conditioned attention, showing that healthy motivation and clinical pathology often differ in degree rather than kind. The framework recasts incubation not as a narrow theory of fear conditioning, but as a domain-general principle governing how recurrent reactivation alters the future significance of psychological representations.
